title: Re-rendering and Performance
summary: See how React renders and commits, what really causes a re-render, and speed up slow screens with structure, memoization, the Compiler, and transitions.
intro: Sooner or later a screen feels slow: the search box lags a beat behind your typing, or a long list stutters when you change a filter. In React the cause is almost always rendering: too much of it, too often, or one slow piece holding up the rest. Most performance advice only makes sense once you have an accurate picture of what React does when state changes, so this lesson builds that picture first: the three steps of every update, how React matches the new screen with the old one, and exactly what makes a component render again. Then come the fixes, in the order teams reach for them: better structure, memoization and the React Compiler, then transitions, code splitting, and long lists.

steps.title: Trigger, render, commit
steps.body:
People say a component re-rendered as if that meant the page changed. It doesn't, and that difference is the key to every fix in this lesson. When state changes, React does its work in three steps, and only the last one touches the page.

```diagram rendering-and-performance-update-steps
React renders and commits, then the browser paints, then your effects run.
```

## Step 1: a trigger

Something has to start an update, and there are only two kinds of start. The first render happens when `createRoot(...).render(...)` in `main.tsx` puts your app on the page. Every update after that starts with a state change: a set function from `useState`, or a `dispatch` from `useReducer`. A context value and a store change, which the Sharing State lesson covered, are state changes too, kept in a different place.

React doesn't start the moment you call a set function. It **batches** them, as the State and Events lesson showed: every update from one event goes into a queue, and React handles the whole queue in one go. Three set calls in one click make one update, not three.

## Step 2: render

**Rendering** means React calls your component functions. It starts at the component whose state changed and calls it with its current props and state. Your function returns JSX, which compiles to **elements**: plain JavaScript objects that describe what should be on the screen, like "a `p` with the text Cart: 1". For every component in that JSX, React calls that component too, and so on down the tree, until it has a complete tree of elements.

Nothing on the screen changes during this step. React is only working out what the screen should look like. That's why components must be pure: React can call them more than once, as StrictMode does on purpose in development, or start a render and throw the result away, which part 6 of this lesson uses.

## Step 3: commit

With the new tree of elements in hand, React compares it with the tree from the last render and works out the smallest set of changes that turns the old DOM into the new one: insert this node, remove that one, change this text, set that attribute. Applying those changes to the DOM is the **commit**. Right after it, React attaches refs and runs layout effects, which the Effects, Refs, and Browser APIs lesson explained.

Then the browser takes over and does what the web course showed it doing after any DOM change: it recalculates styles, lays the page out, and paints the pixels. After the paint, React runs your effects. In the diagram, steps 1 to 3 are React's, step 4 is the browser's, and step 5 is React again.

## Rendering is not updating the DOM

When a render produces the same elements as last time, the commit changes nothing. The example below shows it: one click renders three components, and exactly one piece of text in the DOM changes. React didn't rewrite the heading or the footer with the same words. It left those nodes alone.

So a render is a cost paid in JavaScript time, calling functions and comparing objects, not in work for the browser. Usually it's a small cost: React renders hundreds of small components in a millisecond or two. It becomes a problem in two cases: when one component is slow to render, like one that sorts thousands of products, and when a large part of the tree renders on every key press. The rest of this lesson is about finding and fixing those two cases.

examples.title: One click, three renders, one DOM change
examples.prompt: `src/App.tsx` logs each time a component renders, and an effect starts a `MutationObserver`, the browser API from the web course that reports changes to the DOM. StrictMode is off in `main.tsx`, so each render logs once. These are the lines it logged when the page loaded, then after one click on Add to cart.
examples.output:
render App
render CartBadge
render Footer
render App
render CartBadge
render Footer
DOM change: characterData "1"
examples.explanation:
The first three lines are the first render: React called `App`, then the two components in its JSX. No DOM change was logged then, because the observer only starts in an effect, after that first commit.

The click calls `setCount(1)`, the trigger. React renders `App` again, and since `App`'s JSX holds `CartBadge` and `Footer`, it calls them too, so all three log a second time. Then the commit compares old and new. The heading, the button, and the footer came out exactly as before, so React leaves them. `CartBadge`'s text went from 0 to 1, so React changes that one text node, and the observer reports it: `characterData` is the browser's name for the content of a text node, which is now `1`.

Notice that `Footer` rendered for nothing: its function ran and returned the same JSX as before. Part 3 explains why that happens, and parts 4 and 5 how to skip it when it matters.

steps.title: Reconciliation and identity
steps.body:
A text box that empties itself, a form that still shows the last product's data, an input that loses focus after every key press: these bugs all come from one rule, the one React uses to decide which old component matches which new one. Once you know it, you can predict whether state survives an update.

## Comparing two trees

After a render, React holds two trees of elements: the one from the last commit and the new one. For each element it has to decide: is this the same thing as before, just updated, or something new? Making that decision is called **reconciliation**. Comparing every element with every other one would take far too long on a big page, so React uses two simple rules instead.

1. It compares elements in the same place: the first child with the first child, the second with the second, level by level from the top.
2. If an element has the same **type** as the element in that place before, it's the same thing. The type is the tag, like `li`, or the component function, like `ProductCard`. React keeps it: the DOM node stays, the component keeps its state, and only the props change. If the type is different, React destroys the old one and everything inside it, DOM nodes and state included, runs its effect cleanups, and builds the new one from nothing.

```diagram rendering-and-performance-reconcile
Same type in the same place is kept. A new type replaces the whole branch.
```

In the diagram, a shop page switches from a grid of cards to a table. The header has the same type in the same place, so React keeps it and its state. The grid and the table are different components, so the whole grid branch is destroyed, cards and all, and the table is built fresh.

## State lives in a place, not in your function

Your component function doesn't hold its state. React does, in its own tree of **fibers**: one small object for each component and each DOM element on the screen, holding its current props, its state, its effects, and links to its parent and children. Fiber is the name of React's insides since 2017. When your component calls `useState`, React looks in the fiber at that place in the tree and hands back what's stored there, in the order the hooks were called. That's why hooks must be called in the same order every render: the fiber keeps them as a list.

So a component's identity is its place in the tree plus its type. Two results surprise people:

- **Same type, same place, new props: the state stays.** In `{onSale ? <PriceFilter label="Sale" /> : <PriceFilter label="All" />}`, both branches put a `PriceFilter` in the same place, so React treats them as one component, and whatever the filter held survives the switch.
- **Another type in the same place: the state goes.** Switching `<ProductGrid />` to `<ProductTable />` throws away anything the grid kept, like which card was expanded.

## Keys change the match

In a list, matching by place would pair the wrong items after a reorder, so React matches children by their `key` instead, as the Components, JSX, and Props lesson showed. A key works outside lists too: give an element a new key, and React treats it as a different element in that place, destroying the old one. That's how you reset a component on purpose, like `<ReviewForm key={slug} />` giving every product a fresh form, as in the Effects, Refs, and Browser APIs lesson.

## Never define a component inside another

A function written inside a component is a new function every time that component renders. To React, a new function is a new type. So a component defined inside another one is destroyed and mounted again on every render of its parent: its state is lost, its DOM nodes are replaced, and focus is gone. The example shows the classic symptom, a search box that takes one letter and then stops.

The fix is to move the inner component to the top level of its file and pass it what it needs as props. Then it's the same function on every render, and React keeps it.

examples.title: A component defined inside a component
examples.prompt: `src/features/products/ProductsPage.tsx`, written the wrong way: `SearchBox` is defined inside `ProductsPage`, and an effect logs when it mounts and unmounts. Clicking the box and typing t, then e, logged these lines.
examples.output:
SearchBox mounted
SearchBox unmounted
SearchBox mounted
examples.explanation:
The first line comes from the first render. Typing t calls `setQuery("t")`, so `ProductsPage` renders again, and that render creates a brand-new `SearchBox` function. React finds a different type in the same place, so it unmounts the old `SearchBox`, which runs the effect's cleanup and logs `SearchBox unmounted`, then mounts the new one, which logs `SearchBox mounted`.

The new input shows t, since it reads `query`, but it isn't focused. Focus was on the input React just removed, so the browser moved it to the page itself. The e you typed next went nowhere, and the box still says t.

To fix it, move `SearchBox` out of `ProductsPage`, give it `value` and `onChange` props, and render `<SearchBox value={query} onChange={setQuery} />`. It's then the same function every render, so React keeps the input and its focus.

steps.title: What causes a re-render
steps.body:
Before you speed anything up, you need to know why a component rendered. Most wasted renders come from one rule that surprises almost everyone the first time they see it, so it's worth getting exactly right.

## The four reasons

A component renders again for one of these reasons, and no others:

1. **Its own state changed.** It called a set function from `useState`, or `dispatch` from `useReducer`, with a new value. A value equal to the current one, compared with `Object.is` as the State and Events lesson showed, changes nothing, and React skips the render.
2. **Its parent rendered.** Rendering goes all the way down: when a component renders, React renders every component in the JSX it returned, and every component in theirs.
3. **A context it reads changed.** Every component that reads a context with `use` or `useContext` renders when its provider gets a new value, as the Sharing State lesson showed.
4. **A store value it selects changed.** A Zustand selector returned something different from last time.

## Props are not a reason

It feels natural to think a component renders when its props change. That's not how it works. A child's props can only be new because its parent rendered, and when the parent renders, the child renders too, whether its props changed or not.

The example shows it. Clicking Cart changes `cartOpen`, the state of `ShopPage`, and only `Header` gets a different prop. But `ProductGrid`, its three cards, and `Footer` all render as well, with exactly the same props they had before.

That's React's default, and it's a sensible one. Rendering is usually cheap, and checking every prop of every component costs time too, time that's wasted whenever the props did change. So React renders everything below a change and lets the commit sort out what's different. Parts 4 and 5 show how to skip the branches where that default costs too much.

The example runs with the React Compiler turned off, to show React's own behavior. Your project has the Compiler on, and part 5 shows how it changes this log.

## Seeing renders as they happen

You don't have to add log lines to find out what renders. React DevTools, the browser extension you met when you set up your project, has two tools for it.

- **Highlight updates.** In the Components tab, open the settings (the gear) and turn on Highlight updates when components render. Every component that renders flashes with an outline on the page. Type in a search box and watch: when the whole page lights up on every key press, you've found work worth cutting.
- **The Profiler.** The Profiler tab records while you use the app: press record, do the slow thing, and press stop. It shows each commit, and for each one, which components rendered and how many milliseconds each took. In the Profiler's settings, turn on Record why each component rendered while profiling. Then, when you select a component, it tells you why it rendered, with reasons like Props changed, Hook 1 changed, or The parent component rendered.

Chrome's own Performance panel helps too. Since React 19.2, a recording there includes React's tracks: each render and commit, drawn on the same timeline as the browser's style, layout, and paint. That's the place to look when a click feels slow and you need to know whether the time went to React, to your code, or to the browser.

## Why it matters

Every one of these reasons starts at one component and spreads down. So the question for a slow screen is always the same: which component's state changed, and how much of the tree sits below it? A change near the top of the app renders nearly everything. A change near the bottom renders almost nothing. The next part uses exactly that.

examples.title: Every child renders with its parent
examples.prompt: `src/features/products/ShopPage.tsx`, with every component logging its renders. It ran with the React Compiler and StrictMode turned off. These are the lines it logged: the first render, then one click on Cart.
examples.output:
render ShopPage
render Header
render ProductGrid
render ProductCard ridge-2p-tent
render ProductCard alpine-1p-tent
render ProductCard basecamp-4p-tent
render Footer
render ShopPage
render Header
render ProductGrid
render ProductCard ridge-2p-tent
render ProductCard alpine-1p-tent
render ProductCard basecamp-4p-tent
render Footer
examples.explanation:
The first seven lines are the first render, from `ShopPage` down to `Footer`. The click calls `setCartOpen(true)`, and the second seven lines are the result: all seven components rendered again.

Only `Header` had a reason to. Its `cartOpen` prop went from `false` to `true`, so its button's `aria-expanded` attribute must change. `ProductGrid` got the same `tents` array as before, the very same object, defined once at the top of the file. Each card got the same product object. `Footer` gets no props at all. They rendered anyway, because their parent rendered.

The commit then changed one attribute in the DOM, `aria-expanded`, and nothing else. With three cards that's harmless. With three hundred cards, each one rendering an image, a price, and a rating, a click on Cart would start to feel slow, and that's the kind of case the next two parts fix.

steps.title: Fix the structure first
steps.body:
The cheapest render is the one that never happens. Before you reach for the tools in the next part, look at where your state lives and what sits under it. Moving a piece of state often removes the wasted renders completely, and the code gets simpler, not more complicated.

## Measure before you change anything

Guessing where the time goes is usually wrong, so measure first, and measure the right build. Development mode is several times slower than what your users run: it checks extra things and, with StrictMode, renders everything twice. To measure, run `npm run build`, then `npm run preview`, which serves the built files, and record with the Profiler or the Performance panel there.

Your laptop is also much faster than many of your users' phones. In the Performance panel, set CPU throttling to 4x slowdown to feel what they feel. The number to watch is **INP**, Interaction to Next Paint, from the web course: the time from a tap or a key press to the next frame on screen. Under 200 milliseconds counts as good. Fix the slowest thing first, and leave alone a component that renders in a tenth of a millisecond, however often it does.

## Move state down

State high in the tree renders everything below it whenever it changes. So keep each piece of state in the lowest component that needs it, as the Sharing State lesson said when it talked about putting state where it's used.

Picture a newsletter box at the bottom of the shop page, its email kept in `ShopPage`:

```tsx sketch
export function ShopPage() {
  const [email, setEmail] = useState("");
  // ... the product grid, then the email input with value={email}
}
```

Each key typed into that box sets `ShopPage`'s state, so the whole page renders, grid and all, once per letter. Nothing above the form needs the email. Move the state into a `NewsletterForm` component that holds the input, and typing renders only that form. The first example shows the log.

## Pass JSX as children

Sometimes the state really does have to sit above the slow part. A panel that shows how far you've scrolled has to wrap the content that scrolls. A collapsible section has to wrap what it hides. For those, let the component with the state take the slow content as `children`:

```tsx sketch
<ScrollProgress>
  <ProductGrid />
</ScrollProgress>
```

This works because of who creates the elements. `<ProductGrid />` is written in `ShopPage`, so it's created when `ShopPage` renders. When `ScrollProgress` changes its own state and renders, `ShopPage` doesn't render, so `children` is the very same element object as last time. React checks for that: when it reaches the same element object in the same place, it skips rendering it. The second example shows it: scrolling renders `ScrollProgress` and leaves the grid alone.

## Keep context values stable

The Sharing State lesson showed the same idea for context. A provider whose `value` is a new object on every render makes every component that reads it render too, whenever the provider's own component renders. Keep the value the same object when nothing in it changed, and split fast-changing values, like the text in a search box, into their own context, or into a store where each component picks just the piece it needs.

## Why structure comes first

Each of these fixes removes renders instead of adding checks. Nothing has to compare props, and nothing can go stale. They also make the code clearer, since each piece of state sits next to the only code that uses it. That's why teams try them before the tools in the next part, and why they still matter in a project with the React Compiler, which can skip a component only when its props didn't change.

examples.title: State moved down into the form
examples.prompt: `src/features/products/ShopPage.tsx` again, with the email in the `NewsletterForm` component that uses it. StrictMode and the Compiler were off. It logged these lines on the first render, then after typing one letter in the email box.
examples.output:
render ShopPage
render ProductGrid
render NewsletterForm
render NewsletterForm
examples.explanation:
The first three lines are the first render, top to bottom. Typing one letter calls `setEmail`, which is `NewsletterForm`'s own state, so the update starts at `NewsletterForm`. Its parent `ShopPage` didn't change, and `ProductGrid` is its sibling, not its child, so neither one renders. One letter, one render.

With the email in `ShopPage`, as the sketch above showed, the same letter rendered `ShopPage`, `ProductGrid`, and the form: everything on the page. The fix didn't add any code. It moved two lines into the component that uses them.

examples.title: Slow content passed in as children
examples.prompt: `src/features/products/ShopPage.tsx` with a scroll panel. `ScrollProgress` keeps how far you've scrolled in its own state, and its CSS class gives it a fixed height that scrolls. It logged these lines on the first render, then after one scroll.
examples.output:
render ShopPage
render ScrollProgress
render ProductGrid
render ScrollProgress
examples.explanation:
The first render logs all three. Scrolling fires `onScroll`, which sets `percent`, the state of `ScrollProgress`, and only `ScrollProgress` renders: its progress bar moves, and `ProductGrid` stays as it was.

`ProductGrid` is inside `ScrollProgress` on the page, but it was written, and so created, in `ShopPage`. `ShopPage` didn't render, so `children` held the same element object as before, and React skipped it. Had `ScrollProgress` rendered `<ProductGrid />` itself, every scroll event, dozens a second, would render the whole grid. Reach for this pattern whenever a component's state changes often but most of what it wraps doesn't depend on that state.

steps.title: Memoization and the React Compiler
steps.body:
Sometimes structure can't remove a render: a parent has to change, and a slow child sits right under it. **Memoization** means remembering a result and reusing it while its inputs stay the same, and React has three tools for it. Since React Compiler 1.0 in 2025, a build step can add them for you, which changes how you write React day to day.

## memo: skip a component

`memo` wraps a component and returns one that skips rendering when its props are the same as last time:

```tsx sketch
const ProductGrid = memo(function ProductGrid({ products }: ProductGridProps) {
  // ...
});
```

When the parent renders, React compares each new prop with the old one using `Object.is`. If every prop is equal, React skips this component and everything under it, and reuses what it rendered last time. Comparing prop by prop like this, without looking inside objects, is called a **shallow** comparison.

## Same contents is not the same object

`Object.is` compares objects, arrays, and functions by **reference**: whether they're the very same object in memory, not whether they look alike. `Object.is({}, {})` is `false`, since those are two separate objects. That's where `memo` quietly stops working. A parent that passes `filters={{ category }}` or `onSelect={() => select(slug)}` creates a new object or a new function every time it renders, so the memoized child sees a changed prop every time, and never skips.

## useMemo and useCallback: keep the same object

Two hooks keep a value from one render to the next:

- `useMemo(() => compute(), [a, b])` runs the function, remembers the result, and returns that same result on later renders until `a` or `b` changes. Use it for an expensive calculation, like sorting thousands of products, and for an object you pass to a memoized child.
- `useCallback(fn, [a, b])` does the same for a function: you get the same function object back until a dependency changes.

The list in square brackets works like an effect's dependencies, from the Effects, Refs, and Browser APIs lesson: every value from the component that the code reads goes in it, and each one is compared with `Object.is`. The first example puts all three tools together.

## The React Compiler does this for you

The **React Compiler** is a build step, the Babel plugin your project's Vite config already runs, as the Starting a New React Project lesson showed. It reads each component and hook and adds this caching itself, for values, functions, and JSX alike. When `ShopPage` renders because `cartOpen` changed, the compiled code hands back the same `<ProductGrid products={tents} />` element as last time, since nothing it depends on changed. React reaches the same element object in the same place and skips it, exactly as with `children` in the previous part.

That's why the code in your project has no `memo`, `useMemo`, or `useCallback`, and why you'll rarely write them. The compiler memoizes more precisely than people do, it never forgets a dependency, and the code stays plain. The second example shows the log from part 3's `ShopPage` with the Compiler on.

It only works on code that follows React's rules: components that are pure, hooks called at the top level, props and state never changed in place, refs never read during render. When a component breaks a rule, the compiler leaves that component exactly as you wrote it, and it keeps working, just without the caching. Your project's oxlint rules, like `react/purity` and `react/refs`, point at those spots. To opt one component out on purpose, put the directive `"use no memo"` at the top of its function body.

## When you still write them by hand

- In a project or a library that doesn't run the compiler.
- When a value has to keep its identity for your code to be correct, not only fast, like an object an effect depends on. A `useMemo` there says so plainly, and the compiler respects it.
- In a component the compiler skipped, until you fix whatever rule it breaks.

Don't add them everywhere just in case. Each one costs memory and a comparison on every render, and a wrong dependency list brings back old values.

examples.title: Memoizing by hand
examples.prompt: The same `ShopPage` written for a project without the compiler. With the Compiler and StrictMode off, it logged these lines on the first render, then after one click on Cart.
examples.output:
render ShopPage
render Header
render ProductGrid
render Footer
render ShopPage
render Header
examples.explanation:
Three pieces work together. `memo` wraps `Header`, `ProductGrid`, and `Footer`, so each one skips when its props are equal. `tents` is defined once, outside the component, so `ProductGrid` always gets the same array. And `useCallback` with an empty dependency list keeps `toggleCart` the same function forever, which works because it uses the updater form, `setCartOpen((open) => !open)`, and so reads no state of its own.

After the click, `Header` renders because `cartOpen` really changed. `ProductGrid` and `Footer` are skipped. Drop the `useCallback`, and `Header` still renders, which is fine here. But pass a fresh arrow function to a memoized component whose other props never change, and it renders every time anyway: one new object is enough to defeat `memo`.

examples.title: The same page with the compiler on
examples.prompt: The `ShopPage.tsx` from part 3, unchanged, with no `memo` anywhere, built with the React Compiler that this `vite.config.ts` turns on. StrictMode was off. It logged these lines: the first render, then one click on Cart.
examples.output:
render ShopPage
render Header
render ProductGrid
render ProductCard ridge-2p-tent
render ProductCard alpine-1p-tent
render ProductCard basecamp-4p-tent
render Footer
render ShopPage
render Header
examples.explanation:
The first render is the same seven lines as before: nothing is cached yet, so everything renders. The click is where it differs. Without the compiler, the click rendered all seven components. With it, two: `ShopPage`, whose state changed, and `Header`, whose `cartOpen` prop changed.

The compiled `ShopPage` kept the `<ProductGrid products={tents} />` and `<Footer />` elements from its last render, because nothing they depend on changed, and React skipped both, along with the three cards inside the grid. You got the result of the hand-memoized version without writing `memo` or `useCallback` once.

The `vite.config.ts` above is cut down to the line that matters. Your project's config does the same, plus a few more settings.

steps.title: Keeping big screens responsive
steps.body:
Some updates are big however well you structure them: filtering two thousand products, drawing a chart, opening a screen full of code that hasn't loaded yet. JavaScript in the page runs on one thread, as the web course showed with the event loop, so while React renders, the browser can't respond to the next key press. The tools in this part let the urgent update, the one the user is waiting to see, go first, and the heavy work wait or happen somewhere else. ## Transitions: updates that can wait A **transition** marks a state update as not urgent. You get one from `useTransition`: ```tsx sketch const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition(); // ... startTransition(() => setCategory(next)); ``` React renders a transition at low priority, in small pieces, giving the browser a chance to handle clicks and key presses between them. Fiber makes that possible, since each fiber is a small unit of work React can pause after. If a more urgent update arrives in the middle, React drops the half-done render and starts again with the newest state. Until the transition finishes, the screen keeps showing the old content, and `isPending` is `true`, so you can dim the list or show a small spinner. Never put a text input's own `value` in a transition: what someone types must show at once. ## useDeferredValue: a value that can lag Often the slow part reads a value you don't set in one place, like the search text a controlled input updates. `useDeferredValue` gives you a copy of it that's allowed to lag behind: ```tsx sketch const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query); // ... ``` On each key press, React first renders with the old `deferredQuery`, which is fast, since the results can be skipped, so the input updates at once. Then it renders again in the background with the new value, as a transition. While `query !== deferredQuery`, the results are behind, and you can show that. It only helps when the slow component skips renders whose props didn't change, which the compiler, or `memo`, takes care of. ## Load code when it's needed: lazy and Suspense The web course showed that `import()` splits code into a separate file, a chunk, loaded only when it's asked for. `lazy` turns such a chunk into a component: ```tsx sketch const ReviewEditor = lazy(() => import("@/features/reviews/ReviewEditor")); // ... Loading the editor…

}> setWriting(false)} /> ``` The file has to have a default export, the component. The first time `ReviewEditor` renders, React starts loading its chunk, and something has to show in the meantime. That's the job of **Suspense**: a component that shows its `fallback` while anything inside it is still waiting, here for code, and in the Calling APIs From React lesson, for data. Once the chunk arrives, the editor takes the fallback's place. The first example shows the extra file in a build. ## Long lists: draw only what's visible A list of five thousand reviews makes five thousand sets of DOM nodes, even when twenty fit on the screen. A **virtualized** list renders only the rows in view, plus a few on each side, keeps the scroll bar the right size with empty space, and swaps rows in and out as you scroll. Libraries like TanStack Virtual do the measuring. Reach for one when a list has hundreds of rows or more. For fewer, pages or a Load more button are simpler. ## Hide without unmounting: Activity The Components, JSX, and Props lesson showed that a component you stop rendering loses its state, while one you only hide keeps it. React's `` component, new in React 19.2, makes hiding cheap and safe. With `mode="hidden"`, its content stays mounted with its state, hidden with `display: none`, its effects are cleaned up so nothing runs in the background, and React renders it at the lowest priority, so a tab can be ready before anyone opens it. The second example uses it for a product page's tabs. That's the end of State and Performance. The next lesson starts Building an App, by giving each of the shop's screens its own address with React Router.

examples.explanation:
`tsc -b` checks the types first, then Vite builds. The list at the end is every file in `dist/`, with its size, and its size after gzip compression, which is what travels over the network. `ReviewEditor-voTcZGo_.js` is the editor's own chunk, with a content hash in its name, as the web course explained.

`index-BUBS5aRi.js` is everything else, React included. A visitor who never presses Write a review never downloads the editor. In a real app, the editor might bring a rich-text library weighing hundreds of kilobytes, and splitting it off keeps that weight away from every visitor who only reads.

examples.title: Tabs that keep their state
examples.prompt: `src/features/products/ProductTabs.tsx` puts each tab's content in an `Activity`. With StrictMode off, it logged these lines while you open Reviews, type a draft, switch to Details, and switch back.
examples.output:
ReviewDraft effect: setup
ReviewDraft effect: cleanup
ReviewDraft effect: setup
examples.explanation:
On the first render, the Reviews tab is hidden, but React still renders `ReviewDraft` in the background at low priority. Its effect doesn't run while it's hidden, so nothing logs yet. Clicking Reviews makes it visible, and the effect's setup runs.

Switching to Details hides it again: the effect's cleanup runs, and the textarea gets `display: none`, but the component stays mounted. Switching back runs the setup once more, and the draft is still there, Stayed dry all night, exactly as typed.

With `{tab === "reviews" && <ReviewDraft />}`, the draft would vanish on every switch. With CSS alone, it would survive, but its effects would keep running while hidden. `Activity` gives you the state without the background work.

recap:
- Every update is a trigger, a render that calls your components, and a commit that applies only the DOM changes, then the browser paints.
- A render costs JavaScript time, not DOM work: a render that returns the same elements changes nothing on the page.
- React keeps state by place in the tree and type, so a new type, a new key, or a component defined inside another resets it.
- A component renders when its state, its parent, a context it reads, or a store value it selects changes. Props alone are never the trigger.
- Measure in a production build first, then fix the structure: move state down, and pass slow content in as children.
- memo, useMemo, and useCallback skip work when inputs keep their identity, and the React Compiler adds them for you.
- Transitions and useDeferredValue keep typing fast, lazy with Suspense loads code on demand, and Activity hides without losing state.
